entries.d7c159514f57230b599e395aac8d50664c6ae11e: <div sID="gen15090" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Eccl.10" sID="Eccl.10"/> <div eID="gen15090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15091" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15092" type="x-p"/> This chapter seems to be like Solomon's proverbs, a collection of wise sayings and observations, rather than a part of his sermon; but the preacher studied to be sententious, and "set in order many proverbs," to be brought in in his preaching. Yet the general scope of all the observations in this chapter is to recommend wisdom to us, and its precepts and rules, as of great use for the right ordering of our conversation and to caution us against folly. I. He recommends wisdom to private persons, who are in an inferior station. 1. It is our wisdom to preserve our reputation, in managing our affairs dexterously, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.1-Eccl.10.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. 2. To be submissive to our superiors if at any time we have offended them, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.4">ver. 4</reference>. 3. To live quiet and peaceable lives, and not to meddle with those that are factious and seditious, and are endeavouring to disturb the government and the public repose, the folly and danger of which disloyal and turbulent practices he shows, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.8-Eccl.10.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. 4. To govern our tongues well, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.12-Eccl.10.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. 5. To be diligent in our business and provide well for our families, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.18-Eccl.10.19">ver. 18, 19</reference>. 6. Not to speak ill of our rulers, no, not in secret, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.20">ver. 20</reference>. II. He recommends wisdom to rulers; let them not think that, because their subjects must be quiet under them, therefore they may do what they please; no, but, 1. Let them be careful whom they prefer to places of trust and power, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.5-Eccl.10.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. 2. Let them manage themselves discreetly, be generous and not childish, temperate and not luxurious, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.16-Eccl.10.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>. Happy the nation when princes and people make conscience of their duty according to these rules.
entries.878ca4850320137b5b842b461c9640264d601834: <div eID="gen15092" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15091" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Advantages of Wisdom.</title> <div sID="gen15093" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: <hi type="italic">so doth</hi> a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom <hi type="italic">and</hi> honour. 2 A wise man's heart <hi type="italic">is</hi> at his right hand; but a fool's heart at his left. <hi type="super">3</hi> Yea also, when he that is a fool walketh by the way, his wisdom faileth <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and he saith to every one <hi type="italic">that</hi> he <hi type="italic">is</hi> a fool. <div eID="gen15093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15094" type="x-p"/> In these verses Solomon shows, <div eID="gen15094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15095" type="x-p"/> I. What great need wise men have to take heed of being guilty of any instance of folly; for <hi type="italic">a little folly</hi> is a great blemish to him that <hi type="italic">is in reputation for wisdom and honour,</hi> and is as hurtful to his good name as <hi type="italic">dead flies</hi> are to a sweet perfume, not only spoiling the sweetness of it, but making it <hi type="italic">to send forth a stinking savour.</hi> Note, 1. True wisdom is true honour, and will gain a man a reputation, which is like a box of precious ointment, pleasing and very valuable. 2. The reputation that is got with difficulty, and by a great deal of wisdom, may be easily lost, and by a <hi type="italic">little folly,</hi> because envy fastens upon eminency, and makes the worst of the mistakes and miscarriages of those who are cried up for wisdom, and improves them to their disadvantage; so that the folly which in another would not be taken notice of in them is severely censured. Those who make a great profession of religion have need to walk very circumspectly, to <hi type="italic">abstain from all appearances of evil,</hi> and approaches towards it, because many eyes are upon them, that watch for their halting; their character is soon sullied, and they have a great deal of reputation to lose. <div eID="gen15095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15096" type="x-p"/> II. What a deal of advantage a wise man has above a fool in the management of business (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">A wise man's heart is at his right hand,</hi> so that he goes about his business with dexterity, turns his hand readily to it, and goes through it with despatch; his counsel and courage are ready to him, whenever he has occasion for them. But a <hi type="italic">fool's heart is at his left hand;</hi> it is always to seek when he has any thing to do that is of importance, and therefore he goes awkwardly about it, like a man that is left-handed; he is soon at a loss and at his wits' end. <div eID="gen15096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15097" type="x-p"/> III. How apt fools are at every turn to proclaim their own folly, and expose themselves; he that is either witless or graceless, either silly or wicked, if he be ever so little from under the check, and left to himself, if he but <hi type="italic">walk by the way,</hi> soon shows what he is; his <hi type="italic">wisdom fails him,</hi> and, by some impropriety or other, <hi type="italic">he says to every one he meets that he is a fool</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.3">v. 3</reference>), that is, he discovers his folly as plainly as if he had told them so. He cannot conceal it, and he is not ashamed of it. Sin is the reproach of sinners wherever they go.
entries.bd7dd85beac75bc8dbe849bf59ad2f377d506c4b: <div eID="gen15097" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Mutual Duties of Princes and Subjects.</title> <div sID="gen15098" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place; for yielding pacifieth great offences. 5 There is an evil <hi type="italic">which</hi> I have seen under the sun, as an error <hi type="italic">which</hi> proceedeth from the ruler: <hi type="super">6</hi> Folly is set in great dignity, and the rich sit in low place. <hi type="super">7</hi> I have seen servants upon horses, and princes walking as servants upon the earth. <hi type="super">8</hi> He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it; and whoso breaketh a hedge, a serpent shall bite him. <hi type="super">9</hi> Whoso removeth stones shall be hurt therewith; <hi type="italic">and</hi> he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby. <hi type="super">10</hi> If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> profitable to direct. <hi type="super">11</hi> Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment; and a babbler is no better. <div eID="gen15098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15099" type="x-p"/> The scope of these verses is to keep subjects loyal and dutiful to the government. In Solomon's reign the people were very rich, and lived in prosperity, which perhaps made them proud and petulant, and when the taxes were high, though they had enough to pay them with, it is probable that many conducted themselves insolently towards the government and threatened to rebel. To such Solomon here gives some necessary cautions. <div eID="gen15099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15100" type="x-p"/> I. Let not subjects carry on a quarrel with their prince upon any private personal disgust (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee,</hi> if upon some misinformation given him, or some mismanagement of thine, he is displeased at thee, and threaten thee, yet <hi type="italic">leave not thy place,</hi> forget not the duty of a subject, revolt not from thy allegiance, do not, in a passion, quit thy post in his service and throw up thy commission, as despairing ever to regain his favour. No, wait awhile, and thou wilt find he is not implacable, but that <hi type="italic">yielding pacifies great offences.</hi>" Solomon speaks for himself, and for every wise and good man that is a master, or a magistrate, that he could easily forgive those, upon their submission, whom yet, upon their provocation, he had been very angry with. It is safer and better to yield to an angry prince than to contend with him. <div eID="gen15100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15101" type="x-p"/> II. Let not subjects commence a quarrel with their prince, though the public administration be not in every thing as they would have it. He grants <hi type="italic">there is an evil often seen under the sun,</hi> and it is a king's-evil, an evil which the king only can cure, for <hi type="italic">it is an error which proceeds from the ruler</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.5">v. 5</reference>); it is a mistake which rulers, consulting their personal affections more than the public interests, are too often guilty of, that men are not preferred according to their merit, but <hi type="italic">folly is set in great dignity,</hi> men of shattered brains, and broken fortunes, are put in places of power and trust, while the rich men of good sense and good estates, whose interest would oblige them to be true to the public, and whose abundance would be likely to set them above temptations to bribery and extortion, yet sit in low places, and can get no preferment (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.6">v. 6</reference>), either the ruler knows not how to value them or the terms of preferment are such as they cannot in conscience comply with. It is ill with a people when vicious men are advanced and men of worth are kept under hatches. This is illustrated <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.7">v. 7</reference>. "<hi type="italic">I have seen servants upon horses,</hi> men not so much of mean extraction and education (if that were all, it were the more excusable, nay, there is many a wise servant who with good reason <hi type="italic">has rule over a son that causes shame</hi>), but of sordid, servile, mercenary dispositions. I have seen these riding in pomp and state as princes, while princes, men of noble birth and qualities, fit to rule a kingdom, have been forced to <hi type="italic">walk as servants upon the earth,</hi> poor and despised." Thus God, in his providence, punishes a wicked people; but, as far as it is the ruler's act and deed, it is certainly his <hi type="italic">error,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">great evil,</hi> a grievance to the subject and very provoking; but it is <hi type="italic">an error under the sun,</hi> which will certainly be rectified above the sun, and when it shall shine no more, for in heaven it is only wisdom and holiness that are set in great dignity. But, if the prince be guilty of his error, yet let not the subjects <hi type="italic">leave their place,</hi> nor rise up against the government, nor form any project for the alteration of it; nor let the prince carry on the humour too far, nor set such servants, such beggars, on horseback, as will ride furiously over the ancient land-marks of the constitution, and threaten the subversion of it. <div eID="gen15101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15102" type="x-p"/> 1. Let neither prince nor people violently attempt any changes, nor make a forcible entry upon a national settlement, for they will both find it of dangerous consequence, which he shows here by four similitudes, the scope of which is to give us a caution not to meddle to our own hurt. Let not princes invade the rights and liberties of their subjects; let not subjects mutiny and rebel against their princes; for, (1.) <hi type="italic">He that digs a pit</hi> for another, it is ten to one but he <hi type="italic">falls into it</hi> himself, and his violent dealing returns upon his own head. If princes become tyrants, or subjects become rebels, all histories will tell both what is likely to be their fate and that it is at their utmost peril, and it were better for both to be content within their own bounds. (2.) <hi type="italic">Whoso breaks a hedge,</hi> an old hedge, that has long been a land-mark, let him expect that a <hi type="italic">serpent,</hi> or <hi type="italic">adder,</hi> such as harbour in rotten hedges, will <hi type="italic">bite him;</hi> some viper or other will fasten upon his hand, <reference osisRef="Acts.28.3">Acts xxviii. 3</reference>. God, by his ordinance, as by a hedge, has inclosed the prerogatives and powers of princes; their persons are under his special protection; those therefore that form any treasonable designs against their peace, their crown, and dignity, are but twisting halters for themselves. (3.) <hi type="italic">Whoso removes stones,</hi> to pull down a wall or building, does but pluck them upon himself; he shall be <hi type="italic">hurt therewith,</hi> and will wish that he had let them alone. Those that go about to alter a well-modelled well-settled government, under colour of redressing some grievances and correcting some faults in it, will quickly perceive not only that it is easier to find fault than to mend, to demolish that which is good than to build up that which is better, but that they thrust their own fingers into the fire and overwhelm themselves in the ruin they occasion. (4.) <hi type="italic">He that cleaves the wood,</hi> especially if, as it follows, he has sorry tools (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.10">v. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">shall be endangered thereby;</hi> the chips, or his own axe-head, will fly in his face. If we meet with knotty pieces of timber, and we think to master them by force and violence, and hew them to pieces, they may not only prove too hard for us, but the attempt may turn to our own damage. <div eID="gen15102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15103" type="x-p"/> 2. Rather let both prince and people act towards each other with prudence, mildness, and good temper: <hi type="italic">Wisdom is profitable to direct</hi> the ruler how to manage a people that are inclined to be turbulent, so as neither, on the one hand, by a supine negligence to embolden and encourage them, nor, on the other hand, by rigour and severity to exasperate and provoke them to any seditious practices. It is likewise profitable to direct the subjects how to act towards a prince that is inclined to bear hard upon them, so as not to alienate his affections from them, but to win upon him by humble remonstrances (not insolent demands, such as the people made upon Rehoboam), by patient submissions and peaceable expedients. The same rule is to be observed in all relations, for the preserving of the comfort of them. Let wisdom direct to gentle methods and forbear violent ones. (1.) Wisdom will teach us to whet the tool we are to make use of, rather than, by leaving it blunt, oblige ourselves to exert so much the <hi type="italic">more strength,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.10">v. 10</reference>. We might save ourselves a great deal of labour, and prevent a great deal of danger, if we did whet before we cut, that is, consider and premeditate what is fit to be said and done in every difficult case, that we may accommodate ourselves to it and may do our work smoothly and easily both to others and to ourselves. Wisdom will direct how to sharpen and put an edge upon both ourselves and those we employ, not to <hi type="italic">work deceitfully</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.52.2">Ps. lii. 2</reference>), but to work cleanly and cleverly. The mower loses no time when he is whetting his scythe. (2.) Wisdom will teach us to enchant the serpent we are to contend with, rather than think to out-hiss it (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The serpent will bite</hi> if he be not by singing and music charmed and enchanted, against which therefore he <hi type="italic">stops his ears</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.4-Ps.58.5">Ps. lviii. 4, 5</reference>); <hi type="italic">and a babbler is no better</hi> to all those who enter the lists with him, who therefore must not think by dint of words to out-talk him, but be prudent management to enchant him. <hi type="italic">He that is lord of the tongue</hi> (so the phrase is), a ruler that has liberty of speech and may say what he will, it is as dangerous dealing with him as with a serpent uncharmed; but, if you use the enchantment of a mild and humble submission, you may be safe and out of danger; herein <hi type="italic">wisdom,</hi> the meekness of wisdom, <hi type="italic">is profitable to direct. By long forbearing is a prince persuaded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.25.15">Prov. xxv. 15</reference>. Jacob enchanted Esau with a present and Abigail David. To those that may say any thing it is wisdom to say nothing that is provoking.
entries.157a360a3c5b11753885d9f768615fe757119391: <div eID="gen15103" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Contemptibleness of Folly.</title> <div sID="gen15104" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> The words of a wise man's mouth <hi type="italic">are</hi> gracious; but the lips of a fool will swallow up himself. <hi type="super">13</hi> The beginning of the words of his mouth <hi type="italic">is</hi> foolishness: and the end of his talk <hi type="italic">is</hi> mischievous madness. <hi type="super">14</hi> A fool also is full of words: a man cannot tell what shall be; and what shall be after him, who can tell him? <hi type="super">15</hi> The labour of the foolish wearieth every one of them, because he knoweth not how to go to the city. <div eID="gen15104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15105" type="x-p"/> Solomon, having shown the benefit of wisdom, and of what great advantage it is to us in the management of our affairs, here shows the mischief of folly and how it exposes men, which perhaps comes in as a reflection upon those rulers who <hi type="italic">set folly in great dignity.</hi> <div eID="gen15105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15106" type="x-p"/> I. Fools talk a great deal to no purpose, and they show their folly as much by the multitude, impertinence, and mischievousness of their words, as by any thing; whereas <hi type="italic">the words of a wise man's mouth are gracious,</hi> are grace, manifest grace in his heart and minister grace to the hearers, are good, and such as become him, and do good to all about him, <hi type="italic">the lips of a fool</hi> not only expose him to reproach and make him ridiculous, but <hi type="italic">will swallow up himself</hi> and bring him to ruin, by provoking the government to take cognizance of his seditious talk and call him to an account for it. Adonijah foolishly <hi type="italic">spoke against his own life,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.23">1 Kings ii. 23</reference>. Many a man has been sunk by having <hi type="italic">his own tongue fall upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">Ps. lxiv. 8</reference>. See what a fool's talk is. 1. It takes rise from his own weakness and wickedness: <hi type="italic">The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness,</hi> the foolishness bound up in his heart, that is the corrupt spring out of which all these polluted streams flow, the evil treasure out of which evil things are brought. As soon as he begins to speak you may perceive his folly; at the very first he talks idly, and passionately, and like himself. 2. It rises up to fury, and tends to the hurt and injury of others: <hi type="italic">The end of his talk,</hi> the end it comes to, <hi type="italic">is madness.</hi> He will presently talk himself into an indecent heat, and break out into the wild extravagancies of a distracted man. The end he aims at is mischief; as, at first, he appeared to have little government of himself, so, at last, it appears he has a great deal of malice to his neighbours; that root of bitterness bears gall and wormwood. Note, It is not strange if those that begin foolishly end madly; for an ungoverned tongue, the more liberty is allowed, grows the more violent. 3. It is all the same over and over (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">A fool also is full of words,</hi> a passionate fool especially, that runs on endlessly and never knows when to leave off. He will have the last word, though it be but the same with that which was the first. What is wanting in the weight and strength of his words he endeavours in vain to make up in the number of them; and they must be repeated, because otherwise there is nothing in them to make them regarded. Note, Many who are empty of sense are <hi type="italic">full of words;</hi> and the least solid are the most noisy. The following words may be taken either, (1.) As checking him for his vainglorious boasting in the multitude of his words, what he will do and what he will have, not considering that which every body knows that <hi type="italic">a man cannot tell what shall be</hi> in his own time, while he lives (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.1">Prov. xxvii. 1</reference>), much less can one tell <hi type="italic">what shall be after him,</hi> when he is dead and gone. Would we duly consider our own ignorance of, and uncertainty about, future events, it would cut off a great many of the idle words we foolishly multiply. Or, (2.) As mocking him for his tautologies. He is <hi type="italic">full of words,</hi> for if he do but speak the most trite and common thing, <hi type="italic">a man cannot tell what shall be,</hi> because he loves to hear himself talk, he will say it again, <hi type="italic">what shall be after him who can tell him?</hi> like Battus in Ovid: <div eID="gen15106" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen15107"/> <l level="1" sID="gen15108"/>——————Sub illis<l eID="gen15108" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen15109"/>Montibus (inquit) erant, et erant sub montibus illis—<l eID="gen15109" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen15110"/>Under those mountains were they,<l eID="gen15110" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen15111"/>They were under those mountains, I say—<l eID="gen15111" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen15107"/> <div sID="gen15112" type="x-p"/> II. Fools toil a great deal to no purpose (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.15">v. 15</reference>); <hi type="italic">The labour of the foolish,</hi> to accomplish their designs, <hi type="italic">wearies every one of them.</hi> 1. They weary themselves in that labour which is very foolish and absurd. All their labour is for the world and the body, and the meat that perishes, and in this labour they spend their strength, and exhaust their spirits, and <hi type="italic">weary themselves for very vanity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.13">Hab. ii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa. lv. 2</reference>. They choose that service which is perfect drudgery rather than that which is perfect liberty. 2. That labour which is necessary, and would be profitable, and might be gone through with ease, wearies them, because they go about it awkwardly and foolishly, and so make their business a toil to them, which, if they applied themselves to it prudently, would be a pleasure to them. Many complain of the labours of religion as grievous, which they would have no reason to complain of if the exercises of Christian piety were always under the direction of Christian prudence. The foolish tire themselves in endless pursuits, and never bring any thing to pass, <hi type="italic">because they know not how to go to the city,</hi> that is, because they have not capacity to apprehend the plainest thing, such as the entrance into a great city is, where one would think it were impossible for a man to miss his road. Men's imprudent management of their business robs them both of the comfort and of the benefit of it. But it is the excellency of the way to the heavenly city that it is a high-way, in which the <hi type="italic">wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Isa. xxxv. 8</reference>); yet sinful folly makes men miss that way.
entries.11c78ef974361acbcad78959c23c12209a2450df: <div eID="gen15112" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Mutual Duties of Princes and Subjects.</title> <div sID="gen15113" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Woe to thee, O land, when thy king <hi type="italic">is</hi> a child, and thy princes eat in the morning! <hi type="super">17</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou, O land, when thy king <hi type="italic">is</hi> the son of nobles, and thy princes eat in due season, for strength, and not for drunkenness! <hi type="super">18</hi> By much slothfulness the building decayeth; and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through. 19 A feast is made for laughter, and wine maketh merry: but money answereth all <hi type="italic">things.</hi> <hi type="super">20</hi> Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter. <div eID="gen15113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15114" type="x-p"/> Solomon here observes, <div eID="gen15114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15115" type="x-p"/> I. How much the happiness of a land depends upon the character of its rulers; it is well or ill with the people according as the princes are good or bad. 1. The people cannot be happy when their princes are childish and voluptuous (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Woe unto thee, O land!</hi> even the land of Canaan itself, though otherwise the glory of all lands, when <hi type="italic">thy king is a child,</hi> not so much in age (Solomon himself was young when his kingdom was happy in him) as in understanding; when the prince is weak and foolish as a child, fickle and fond of changes, fretful and humoursome, easily imposed upon, and hardly brought to business, it is ill with the people. The body staggers if the head be giddy. Perhaps Solomon wrote this with a foresight of his son Rehoboam's ill conduct (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.7">2 Chron. xiii. 7</reference>); he was a child all the days of his life and his family and kingdom fared the worse for it. Nor is it much better with a people when their princes <hi type="italic">eat in the morning,</hi> that is, make a god of their belly and make themselves slaves to their appetites. If the king himself be a child, yet if the princes and privy-counsellors are wise and faithful, and apply themselves to business, the land may do the better; but if they addict themselves to their pleasures, and prefer the gratifications of the flesh before the despatch of the public business, which they disfit themselves for by eating and drinking <hi type="italic">in a morning,</hi> when judges are epicures, and do not eat to live, but live to eat, what good can a nation expect! 2. The people cannot but be happy when their rulers are generous and active, sober and temperate, and men of business, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.17">v. 17</reference>. The land is then blessed, (1.) When the sovereign is governed by principles of honour, <hi type="italic">when the king is the son of nobles,</hi> actuated and animated by a noble spirit, which scorns to do any thing base and unbecoming so high a character, which is solicitous for the public welfare, and prefers that before any private interests. Wisdom, virtue, and the fear of God, beneficence, and a readiness to do good to all mankind, these ennoble the royal blood. 2. When the subordinate magistrates are more in care to discharge their trusts than to gratify their appetites; when they <hi type="italic">eat in due season</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.15">Ps. cxlv. 15</reference>); let us not take ours unseasonable, lest we lose the comfort of seeing God give it to us. Magistrates should <hi type="italic">eat for strength,</hi> that their bodies may be fitted to serve their souls in the service of God and their country, <hi type="italic">and not for drunkenness,</hi> to make themselves unfit to do any thing either for God or man, and particularly to <hi type="italic">sit in judgment,</hi> for they will <hi type="italic">err through wine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.7">Isa. xxviii. 7</reference>), will <hi type="italic">drink and forget the law,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.5">Prov. xxxi. 5</reference>. It is well with a people when their princes are examples of temperance, when those that have most to spend upon themselves know how to deny themselves. <div eID="gen15115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15116" type="x-p"/> II. Of what ill consequence slothfulness is both to private and public affairs (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">By much slothfulness and idleness of the hands,</hi> the neglect of business, and the love of ease and pleasure, <hi type="italic">the building decays, drops through</hi> first, and by degrees drops down. If it be not kept well covered, and care be not taken to repair the breaches, as any happen, it will rain in, and the timber will rot, and the house will become unfit to dwell in. It is so with the family and the affairs of it; if men cannot find in their hearts to take pains in their callings, to tend their shops and look after their own business, they will soon run in debt and go behind-hand, and, instead of making what they have more for their children, will make it less. It is so with the public; if the king be <hi type="italic">a child</hi> and will take no care, if the <hi type="italic">princes eat in the morning</hi> and will take no pains, the affairs of the nation suffer loss, and its interests are prejudiced, its honour is sullied, its power is weakened, its borders are encroached upon, the course of justice is obstructed, the treasure is exhausted, and all its foundations are out of course, and all this through the slothfulness of self-seeking of those that should be the <hi type="italic">repairers of its breaches and the restorers of paths to dwell in,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.58.12">Isa. lviii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen15116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15117" type="x-p"/> III. How industrious generally all are, both princes and people, to get money, because that serves for all purposes, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.19">v. 19</reference>. He seems to prefer money before mirth: <hi type="italic">A feast is made for laughter,</hi> not merely for eating, but chiefly for pleasant conversation and the society of friends, not the laughter of the fool, which is madness, but that of wise men, by which they fit themselves for business and severe studies. Spiritual feasts are made for spiritual laughter, holy joy in God. <hi type="italic">Wine makes merry, makes glad the</hi> life, <hi type="italic">but money</hi> is the measure of all things and <hi type="italic">answers all things. Pecuniæ obediunt omnia—Money commands all things.</hi> Though <hi type="italic">wine make merry,</hi> it will not be a house for us, nor a bed, nor clothing, nor provisions and portions for children; <hi type="italic">but money,</hi> if men have enough of it, will be all these. The feast cannot be made without money, and, though men have wine, they are not so much disposed to be merry unless they have money for the necessary supports of life. Money of itself answers nothing; it will neither feed nor clothe; but, as it is the instrument of commerce, it answers all the occasions of this present life. What is to be had may be had for money. But it answers nothing to the soul; it will not procure the pardon of sin, the favour of God, the peace of conscience; the soul, as it is not redeemed, so it is not maintained, with <hi type="italic">corruptible things as silver and gold.</hi> Some refer this to rulers; it is ill with the people when they give up themselves to luxury and riot, feasting and making merry, not only because their business is neglected, but because money must be had to <hi type="italic">answer all</hi> these <hi type="italic">things,</hi> and, in order to that, the people squeezed by heavy taxes. <div eID="gen15117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15118" type="x-p"/> IV. How cautious subjects have need to be that they harbour not any disloyal purposes in their minds, nor keep up any factious cabals or consultations against the government, because it is ten to one that they are discovered and brought to light, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.20">v. 20</reference>. "Though rulers should be guilty of some errors, yet be not, upon all occasions, arraigning their administration and running them down, but make the best of them." Here, 1. The command teaches us our duty "<hi type="italic">Curse not the king, no, not in thy thought,</hi> do not wish ill to the government in thy mind." All sin begins there, and therefore the first risings of it must be curbed and suppressed, and particularly that of treason and sedition. "<hi type="italic">Curse not the rich,</hi> the princes and governors, <hi type="italic">in thy bed-chamber,</hi> in a conclave or club of persons disaffected to the government; associate not with such; <hi type="italic">come not into their secret;</hi> join not with them in speaking ill of the government or plotting against it." 2. The reason consults our safety. "Though the design be carried on ever so closely, <hi type="italic">a bird of the air shall carry the voice</hi> to the king, who has more spies about than thou art aware of, <hi type="italic">and that which has wings shall tell the matter,</hi> to thy confusion and ruin." God sees what men do, and hears what they say, in secret; and, when he pleases, he can bring it to light by strange and unsuspected ways. Wouldst <hi type="italic">thou then not be</hi> hurt by <hi type="italic">the powers</hi> that be, nor <hi type="italic">be afraid of</hi> them? <hi type="italic">Do that which is good and thou shalt have praise of the same; but, if thou do that which is evil, be afraid,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.13.3-Rom.13.4">Rom. xiii. 3, 4</reference>.  <chapter eID="Eccl.10"/> <div eID="gen15118" type="x-p"/>

entries.c5e7db136d7ced3b9b13860b54f0850627cc2743: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8149"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <div sID="gen12716" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.1-Eccl.10.20">Ec 10:1-20</reference>.<div eID="gen12716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12717" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8149"/>1. Following up <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.18">Ec 9:18</reference>.<div eID="gen12717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him that is in reputation--</hi>for example, David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.14">2Sa 12:14</reference>); Solomon (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.1-1Kgs.11.43">1Ki 11:1-43</reference>); Jehoshaphat (2Ch 18:1-34; 19:2); Josiah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.35.22">2Ch 35:22</reference>). The more delicate the perfume, the more easily spoiled is the ointment. Common oil is not so liable to injury. So the higher a man's religious character is, the more hurt is caused by a sinful folly in him. Bad savor is endurable in oil, but not in what professes to be, and is compounded by the perfumer ("apothecary") for, fragrance. "Flies" answer to "a little folly" (sin), appropriately, being small (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.6">1Co 5:6</reference>); also, "Beelzebub" means prince of flies. "Ointment" answers to "reputation" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Ec 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.34.30">Ge 34:30</reference>). The verbs are singular, the noun plural, implying that each of the flies causes the stinking savor. <div eID="gen12718" type="x-p"/>
entries.7da30d7a16d1298cc080d0df00b4ea2caf2e4926: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8150"/><div sID="gen12719" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8150"/>2. (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.14">Ec 2:14</reference>).<div eID="gen12719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12720" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">right--</hi>The right hand is more expert than the left. The godly wise is more on his guard than the foolish sinner, though at times he slip. Better a diamond with a flaw, than a pebble without one. <div eID="gen12720" type="x-p"/>
entries.318c42b936cfbc49ef0ad861c5de541b1d39de3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8151"/><div sID="gen12721" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8151"/><hi type="bold">3. by the way--</hi>in his ordinary course; in his simplest acts (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.12-Prov.6.14">Pr 6:12-14</reference>). That he "saith," virtually, "that he" himself, &c. [Septuagint]. But Vulgate, "He thinks that every one (else whom he meets) is a fool." <div eID="gen12721" type="x-p"/>
entries.a693d423017e999e0c67da4c81ed79d9b074fef8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8152"/><div sID="gen12722" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8152"/><hi type="bold">4. spirit--</hi>anger.<div eID="gen12722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yielding pacifieth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.15.1">Pr 15:1</reference>). This explains "leave not thy place"; do not in a resisting spirit withdraw from thy post of duty (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.3">Ec 8:3</reference>). <div eID="gen12723" type="x-p"/>
entries.28581600b0021d4a0aa98403683a61688e889dd2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8153"/><div sID="gen12724" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8153"/><hi type="bold">5. as--</hi>rather, "by reason of an error" [Maurer and Holden]. <div eID="gen12724" type="x-p"/>
entries.31a51b5a3271f3f8e20c822d9a6de0cc2d40bde8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8154"/><div sID="gen12725" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8154"/><hi type="bold">6. rich--</hi>not in mere wealth, but in wisdom, as the antithesis to "folly" (for "foolish men") shows. So Hebrew, rich, equivalent to "liberal," in a good sense (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.5">Is 32:5</reference>). Mordecai and Haman (<reference osisRef="Esth.3.1">Es 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.6-2Cor.6.11">2; 6:6-11</reference>). <div eID="gen12725" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf91929539c0c09be52937c505557e4729b821bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8155"/><div sID="gen12726" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8155"/><hi type="bold">7. servants upon horses--</hi>the worthless exalted to dignity (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.25">Jr 17:25</reference>); and vice versa (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>). <div eID="gen12726" type="x-p"/>
entries.375bcf48f9191f4afeeaeb9bcdfa8577def8c52b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8156"/><div sID="gen12727" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8156"/>8. The fatal results to kings of such an unwise policy; the wrong done to others recoils on themselves (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.9">Ec 8:9</reference>); they fall into the pit which they dug for others (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.10">Es 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.7.15">Psa 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.26.27">Pr 26:27</reference>). Breaking through the wise fences of their throne, they suffer unexpectedly themselves; as when one is stung by a serpent lurking in the stones of his neighbor's garden wall (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.12">Psa 80:12</reference>), which he maliciously pulls down (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.19">Am 5:19</reference>). <div eID="gen12727" type="x-p"/>
entries.80ab979a2efb8cdba20a2e0699fed42e4be6ae94: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8157"/><div sID="gen12728" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8157"/><hi type="bold">9. removeth stones--</hi>namely, of an ancient building [Weiss]. His neighbor's landmarks [Holden]. Cuts out from the quarry [Maurer].<div eID="gen12728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12729" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">endangered--</hi>by the splinters, or by the head of the hatchet, flying back on himself. Pithy aphorisms are common in the East. The sense is: Violations of true wisdom recoil on the perpetrators. <div eID="gen12729" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e70b26190d07ff11c49de82498242e8d0b08e82: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8158"/><div sID="gen12730" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8158"/><hi type="bold">10. iron ... blunt--</hi>in "cleaving wood" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.9">Ec 10:9</reference>), answering to the "fool set in dignity" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.6">Ec 10:6</reference>), who wants sharpness. More force has then to be used in both cases; but "force" without judgment "endangers" one's self. Translate, "If one hath blunted his iron" [Maurer]. The preference of rash to judicious counsellors, which entailed the pushing of matters by force, proved to be the "hurt" of Rehoboam (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.1-1Kgs.12.33">1Ki 12:1-33</reference>).<div eID="gen12730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wisdom is profitable to direct--</hi>to a prosperous issue. Instead of forcing matters by main "strength" to one's own hurt (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.16">Ec 9:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.18">18</reference>). <div eID="gen12731" type="x-p"/>
entries.c78f71f88a0d10918aed6337a87483a4da3fc389: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8159"/><div sID="gen12732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8159"/>11. A "serpent will bite" if "enchantment" is not used; "and a babbling calumniator is no better." Therefore, as one may escape a serpent by charms (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.4">Psa 58:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.58.5">5</reference>), so one may escape the sting of a calumniator by discretion (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.12">Ec 10:12</reference>), [Holden]. Thus, "without enchantment" answers to "not whet the edge" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.10">Ec 10:10</reference>), both expressing, figuratively, want of judgment. Maurer translates, "There is no gain to the enchanter" (Margin, "master of the tongue") from his enchantments, because the serpent bites before he can use them; hence the need of continual caution. <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.8-Eccl.10.10">Ec 10:8-10</reference>, caution in acting; <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.11">Ec 10:11</reference> and following verses, caution in speaking. <div eID="gen12732" type="x-p"/>
entries.552f8526de3b6ba4bfd9393606751e6db6cd098d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8160"/><div sID="gen12733" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8160"/><hi type="bold">12. gracious--</hi>Thereby he takes precaution against sudden injury (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.11">Ec 10:11</reference>).<div eID="gen12733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12734" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">swallow up himself--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.10.8">Pr 10:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.21">14, 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.32">32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.12.13">12:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.15.2">15:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.11">22:11</reference>). <div eID="gen12734" type="x-p"/>
entries.09540bce8cd0cde04c3315a01ef222e76bfacdaf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8161"/><div sID="gen12735" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8161"/>13. Illustrating the folly and injuriousness of the fool's words; last clause of <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.12">Ec 10:12</reference>. <div eID="gen12735" type="x-p"/>
entries.187e45b811e49feaa384c01e57c2db6396e10776: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8162"/><div sID="gen12736" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8162"/><hi type="bold">14. full of words--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.2">Ec 5:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12737" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a man cannot tell what shall be--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">Ec 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.12">6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.7">8:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">11:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.27.1">Pr 27:1</reference>). If man, universally (including the wise man), cannot foresee the future, much less can the fool; his "many words" are therefore futile. <div eID="gen12737" type="x-p"/>
entries.4bd8f48f1a3c11d7c0d35b0761bb954bb953b595: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8163"/><div sID="gen12738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8163"/><hi type="bold">15. labour ... wearieth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Is 55:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.13">Ha 2:13</reference>).<div eID="gen12738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knoweth not how to go to the city--</hi>proverb for ignorance of the most ordinary matters (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.3">Ec 10:3</reference>); spiritually, the heavenly city (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.7">Psa 107:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.7.13">Mt 7:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.14">14</reference>). Maurer connects <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.15">Ec 10:15</reference> with the following verses. The labor (vexation) caused by the foolish (injurious princes, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.4-Eccl.10.7">Ec 10:4-7</reference>) harasses him who "knows not how to go to the city," to ingratiate himself with them there. English Version is simpler. <div eID="gen12739" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f01c07ba8f456a45f847f973805730276052266: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8164"/><div sID="gen12740" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8164"/><hi type="bold">16. a child--</hi>given to pleasures; behaves with childish levity. Not in years; for a nation may be happy under a young prince, as Josiah.<div eID="gen12740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12741" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eat in the morning--</hi>the usual time for dispensing justice in the East (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.12">Jr 21:12</reference>); here, given to feasting (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Is 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.15">Ac 2:15</reference>). <div eID="gen12741" type="x-p"/>
entries.e142cfd41a2baef117912b1f5a46268101520f53: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8165"/><div sID="gen12742" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8165"/><hi type="bold">17. son of nobles--</hi>not merely in blood, but in virtue, the true nobility (<reference osisRef="Song.7.1">So 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.5">Is 32:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.8">8</reference>).<div eID="gen12742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12743" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in due season--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1">Ec 3:1</reference>), not until duty has first been attended to.<div eID="gen12743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for strength--</hi>to refresh the body, not for revelry (included in "drunkenness"). <div eID="gen12744" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab6a697a61984d42c0128835c066d7a58fa6a550: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8166"/><div sID="gen12745" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8166"/><hi type="bold">18. building--</hi>literally, "the joining of the rafters," namely, the kingdom (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.16">Ec 10:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.6">Is 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.11">Am 9:11</reference>).<div eID="gen12745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12746" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hands--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.5">Ec 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.6.10">Pr 6:10</reference>).<div eID="gen12746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">droppeth--</hi>By neglecting to repair the roof in time, the rain gets through. <div eID="gen12747" type="x-p"/>
entries.30d599aaf29206fe80e66c13ebd130b093b910f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8167"/><div sID="gen12748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8167"/>19. Referring to <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.18">Ec 10:18</reference>. Instead of repairing the breaches in the commonwealth (equivalent to "building"), the princes "make a feast for laughter (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.16">Ec 10:16</reference>), and wine maketh their life glad (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.15">Psa 104:15</reference>), and (but) money supplieth (answereth their wishes by supplying) all things," that is, they take bribes to support their extravagance; and hence arise the wrongs that are perpetrated (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.5">Ec 10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.23">Is 1:23</reference>; 5:23). Maurer takes "all things" of the wrongs to which princes are instigated by "money"; for example, the heavy taxes, which were the occasion of Rehoboam losing ten tribes (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.4">1Ki 12:4</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen12748" type="x-p"/>
entries.e76b0cd3afa1d4d2603f4940b5dc07ede9091e43: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8168"/><div sID="gen12749" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8168"/><hi type="bold">20. thought--</hi>literally, "consciousness."<div eID="gen12749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rich--</hi>the great. The language, as applied to earthly princes knowing the "thought," is figurative. But it literally holds good of the King of kings (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.1-Ps.139.24">Psa 139:1-24</reference>), whose consciousness of every evil thought we should ever realize.<div eID="gen12750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bed-chamber--</hi>the most secret place (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.12">2Ki 6:12</reference>).<div eID="gen12751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12752" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bird of the air, &c.--</hi>proverbial (compare <reference osisRef="Hab.2.11">Ha 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.40">Lu 19:40</reference>); in a way as marvellous and rapid, as if birds or some winged messenger carried to the king information of the curse so uttered. In the East superhuman sagacity was attributed to birds (see on <reference osisRef="Job.28.21">Job 28:21</reference>; hence the proverb). <chapter eID="Eccl.10"/>

entries.cfe48390a49aaf1e5f4f672e8dc48f5da0e8b0a6: <div eID="gen25669" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen25670" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25671" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25671" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25670" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25672" type="x-p"/> Observations on wisdom and folly, <reference osisRef="Ecc.10.1-Ecc.10.3">Ecc 10:1-3</reference>. Concerning right conduct towards rulers, <reference osisRef="Ecc.10.4">Ecc 10:4</reference>. Merit depressed, and worthlessness exalted, <reference osisRef="Ecc.10.5-Ecc.10.7">Ecc 10:5-7</reference>. Of him who digs a pit and removes a landmark, <reference osisRef="Ecc.10.8">Ecc 10:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.10.9">Ecc 10:9</reference>. The use of wisdom and experience, <reference osisRef="Ecc.10.10">Ecc 10:10</reference>. Of the babbler and the fool, <reference osisRef="Ecc.10.11-Ecc.10.15">Ecc 10:11-15</reference>. The infant king, <reference osisRef="Ecc.10.16">Ecc 10:16</reference>. The well-regulated court, <reference osisRef="Ecc.10.17">Ecc 10:17</reference>. Of slothfulness, <reference osisRef="Ecc.10.18">Ecc 10:18</reference>. Of feasting, <reference osisRef="Ecc.10.19">Ecc 10:19</reference>. Speak not evil of the king, <reference osisRef="Ecc.10.20">Ecc 10:20</reference>. <div eID="gen25672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25673" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen25673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25674" type="x-p"/> Dead flies - Any putrefaction spoils perfume; and so a foolish act ruins the character of him who has the reputation of being wise and good. Alas! alas! in an unguarded moment how many have tarnished the reputation which they were many years in acquiring! Hence, no man can be said to be safe, till he is taken to the paradise of God.
entries.49f8922c98febcdabb40f208a96c73fc13da8d3f: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen25674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25675" type="x-p"/> A wise man's heart is at his right hand - As the right hand is ordinarily the best exercised, strongest, and most ready, and the left the contrary, they show, <div eID="gen25675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25676" type="x-p"/> 1. The command which the wise man has over his own mind, feelings, passions, etc., and the prudence with which he acts. And, <div eID="gen25676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25677" type="x-p"/> 2. The want of prudence and management in the fool, who has no restraint on his passions, and no rule or guard upon his tongue. The right hand and the left are used in Scripture to express good and evil. The wise man is always employed in doing good; the fool, in nonsense or evil.
entries.cfc94d5e70a77bbcd0426f901c23a3f9fca307a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen25677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25678" type="x-p"/> When - a fool walketh by the way - In every act of life, and in every company he frequents, the irreligious man shows what he is. Vanity, nonsense, and wickedness are his themes: so that in effect he saith to every one that he is a fool.
entries.e1cf660ca76b1f4e2b779fa3230b15f3d57415cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen25678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25679" type="x-p"/> If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee - If the king get incensed against thee. <div eID="gen25679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25680" type="x-p"/> Leave not thy place - Humble thyself before him, that is thy place and duty; for yielding to him, and not standing stoutly in thy defense, pacifieth great offenses: and then, when his anger is appeased, he will hear any thing in thy justification, if thou have any thing to offer. This is good advice to a child in reference to his parents, and to an inferior of any kind in reference to his superiors. <div eID="gen25680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25681" type="x-p"/> Several of the fathers understood this differently, It the spirit of the ruler - the influence of Satan - hath risen up against and prevailed over thee, to bring thee into some sin; leave not thy place - do not despair of God's mercy; humble thyself before him, and seek pardon through the Son of his love, and this will be מרפא marpe, a remedy or cure even for חטאים גדולים chataim gedolim, great errors or sins. All this is true in itself, whether found in this text or not.
entries.fa49abdb8d175bbb7694e0eff97cd8facbb242c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen25681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25682" type="x-p"/> An error which proceedeth from the ruler - What this error in the ruler is, the two following verses point out: it is simpiy this - an injudicious distribution of offices, and raising people to places of trust and confidence, who are destitute of merit, are neither of name nor family to excite public confidence, and are without property; so that they have no stake in the country, and their only solicitude must naturally be to enrich themselves, and provide for their poor relatives. This is frequent in the governments of the world; and favouritism has often brought prosperous nations to the brink of ruin. Folly was set in dignity; the man of property, sense, and name, in a low place. Servants - menial men, rode upon horses - carried every thing with a high and proud hand; and princes, - the nobles of the people, were obliged to walk by their sides, and often from the state of things to become in effect their servants. This was often the case in this country, during the reign of Thomas a Becket, and Cardinal Woolsey. These insolent men lorded it over the whole nation; and the people and their gentry were raised or depressed according as their pride and caprice willed. And, through this kind of errors, not only a few sovereigns have had most uncomfortable and troublesome reigns, but some have even lost their lives.
entries.08496c729f8c9ee6e28e73d5045f49640a640ff6: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen25682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25683" type="x-p"/> Whoso breaketh a hedge, a serpent shall bite him - While spoiling his neighbor's property, he himself may come to greater mischief: while pulling out the sticks, he may be bit by a serpent, who has his nest there. Some have supposed that נחש nachash here means a thorn; perhaps from the similarity of its prick to the serpent's sting. He who forces his way through a hedge will be pricked by the thorns.
entries.9860af28f8cd211010c745d057b40986cc14d3b6: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen25683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25684" type="x-p"/> Whoso removeth stones - This verse teaches care and caution. Whoever pulls down an old building is likely to be hurt by the stones; and in cleaving wood many accidents occur for want of sufficient caution.
entries.5777e500ed8795f28a1a6c18be527bb155d40920: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen25684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25685" type="x-p"/> If the iron be blunt - If the axe have lost its edge, and the owner do not sharpen it, he must apply the more strength to make it cut: but the wisdom that is profitable to direct will teach him, that he should whet his axe, and spare his strength. Thus, without wisdom and understanding we cannot go profitably through the meanest concerns in life.
entries.dbb29d4b8187a8513b6a8b82bef763bccaf3bbc0: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen25685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25686" type="x-p"/> The serpent will bite without enchantment - בלא לחש belo lachash, without hissing. As a snake may bite before it hiss, so also will the babbler, talkative person, or calumniator. Without directly speaking evil, he insinuates, by innuendoes, things injurious to the reputation of his neighbor. Gif the eddir bite in silence, noyhing lasse than he hath that privily backbiteth - Old MS. Bible. "A babbler of his tongue is no better than a serpent that styngeth without hyssynge." - Coverdale. The moral of this saying is simply this: A calumniator is as dangerous as a poisonous serpent; and from the envenomed tongue of slander and detraction no man is safe. The comparing the serpent, נחש nachash, to a babbler, has something singular in it. I have already supposed that the creature mentioned, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.1">Gen 3:1</reference>, was of the genus simia. This has been ridiculed, but not disproved.
entries.758b23d998ded9d506aa8662f67f4d8a1017f659: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen25686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25687" type="x-p"/> The words of a wise man's mouth - Every thing that proceeds from him is decent and orderly, creditable to himself, and acceptable to those who hear him. But the lips of the fool, which speak every thing at random, and have no understanding to guide them, are not only not pleasant to others, but often destructive to himself.
entries.dcaceb20c4b31221daa19b5de2351bcc719d8b74: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen25687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25688" type="x-p"/> A man cannot tell what shall be - A foolish babbling man will talk on every subject, though he can say as little on the past, as he can on the future.
entries.a7e673584e53428043b78e9e68ef1f40bbf021a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen25688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25689" type="x-p"/> He knoweth not how to go to the city - I suppose this to be a proverb: "He knows nothing; he does not know his way to the next village." He may labor; but for want of judgment he wearies himself to no purpose.
entries.24046cab36672a378ec09cb7b35baa25e00b9084: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen25689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25690" type="x-p"/> Wo to thee, O land, when thy king is a child - Minorities are, in general, very prejudicial to a state. Regents either disagree, and foment civil wars; or oppress the people. Various discordant interests are raised up in a state during a minority; and the young king, having been under the tutelage of interested men, acts partially and injuriously to the interests of the people when he comes to the throne; and this produces popular discontent, and a troubled reign. <div eID="gen25690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25691" type="x-p"/> Thy princes eat in the morning! - They do nothing in order; turn night into day, and day into night; sleep when they should wake, and wake when they should sleep; attending more to chamberings and banquetings, than to the concerns of the state.
entries.70ebb2d9cc3241c63098263a7e5bd7b9eb9d99e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen25691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25692" type="x-p"/> When thy king is the son of nobles - uiov eleuyerwn, the son of freemen; persons well acquainted with the principles of civil liberty, and who rule according to them - Septuagint. Such a one as comes to the throne in a legitimate way, from an ancient regal family, whose right to the throne is incontestable. It requires such a long time to establish a regal right, that the state is in continual danger from pretenders and usurpers, where the king is not the son of nobles. <div eID="gen25692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25693" type="x-p"/> And thy princes eat in due season - All persons in places of trust for the public weal, from the king to the lowest public functionary, should know, that the public are exceedingly scandalized at repeated accounts of entertainments, where irregularity prevails, much money is expended, and no good done. These things are drawn into precedent, and quoted to countenance debauch in the inferior classes. The natural division of the day for necessary repasts is, Breakfast, eight, or half after; Dinner, one, or half after; Supper, eight, or half after. And these, or even earliers hours were formerly observed in these countries. Then we had scarcely any such thing as gout, and no nervous disorders. <div eID="gen25693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25694" type="x-p"/> In ancient nations the custom was to eat but once, and then about mid-day.
entries.014600e0e09369a91a5333f4a360ef51b29ffea5: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen25694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25695" type="x-p"/> By much slothfulness - This is remarkably the case in some countries. Houses are not repaired till they almost fall about the ears of the inhabitants. We have an adage that applies to all such cases: "A stitch in time saves nine."
entries.2bd491d784b9b956a25a9e39b43d46983f7d9d44: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen25695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25696" type="x-p"/> A feast is made for laughter - The object of it is to produce merriment, to banish care and concern of every kind. But who are they who make and frequent such places? Epicures and drunkards generally; such as those of whom Horace speaks: <div eID="gen25696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25697" type="x-p"/> Nos numerus sumus, et fruges consumere nati. <div eID="gen25697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25698" type="x-p"/> Epist. lib. i., ep. 2, ver. 27. "Those whose names stand as indications of men, the useless many; and who appear to be born only to consume the produce of the soil." <div eID="gen25698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25699" type="x-p"/> But money answereth all - This saying has prevailed everywhere. <div eID="gen25699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25700" type="x-p"/> Scilicet uxorem cum dote, fidemque, et amicos, <div eID="gen25700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25701" type="x-p"/> Et genus, et formam Regina Pecunia donat; <div eID="gen25701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25702" type="x-p"/> Ac bene nummatum decorat Suadela, Venusque. <div eID="gen25702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25703" type="x-p"/> Hor. Ep. lib. i., ep. 6, ver. 36. "For gold, the sovereign Queen of all below, <div eID="gen25703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25704" type="x-p"/> Friends, honor, birth, and beauty, can bestow. <div eID="gen25704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25705" type="x-p"/> The goddess of persuasion forms her train; <div eID="gen25705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25706" type="x-p"/> And Venus decks the well-bemonied swain." <div eID="gen25706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25707" type="x-p"/> Francis.
entries.7824d203ace2867dc22ca1e44d5b2ecd9b358e71: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen25707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25708" type="x-p"/> Curse not the king - Do not permit thyself even to think evil of the king; lest thy tongue at some time give vent to thy thoughts, and so thou be chargeable with treason. <div eID="gen25708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25709" type="x-p"/> For a bird of the air shall carry the voice - Does he refer here to such fowls as the carrier pigeon, which were often used to carry letters under their wings to a great distance, and bring back answers? The Targum turns it curiously: "Do not speak evil of the king in thy conscience, nor in the secret of thy heart, nor in the most hidden place in thy house, curse not a wise man; for Raziel calls daily from heaven upon Mount Horeb, and his voice goes through the whole world; and Elijah, the great priest, goes, flying through the air like a winged eagle, and publishes the words which are spoken in secret by all the inhabitants of the earth." <div eID="gen25709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25710" type="x-p"/> Civil government is so peculiarly of God, that he will have it supported for the benefit of mankind; and those who attempt to disturb it are generally marked by his strong disapprobation. And though there have been multitudes of treasons hatched in the deepest secrecy; yet, through the providence of God, they have been discovered in the most singular manner. This shows God's care for government.  <chapter eID="Eccl.10"/> <div eID="gen25710" type="x-p"/>

entries.ae4b082472c1cff207aa4fb9047474329c912d34: <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.1">Ecc 10:1</reference> <div eID="gen12364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12365" type="x-p"/> The second half of the foregoing double proverb introduces what now follows: “Poisonous flies make to stink, make to ferment the oil of the preparer of ointment; heavier than wisdom, than honour, weighs a little folly.” We do not need to change מות זבוּבי, on account of the foll. sing. of the pred., either into זבוגי ם (as possible by Hitz.) or זב ימוּתי (Luzz.); both are inadmissible, for the style of Koheleth is not adorned with archaisms such as <hi type="italic">Chirek compaginis</hi>; and also such an attrib. clause as זבוב ימות, a fly which dies,” is for him too refined; but both are also unnecessary, for a plur. of the subj., in which the plurality of the individuals comes less into view than the oneness of their character, is frequently enough followed by the sing. of the pred., <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.39.22">Gen 39:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.1.20">Joe 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.12">Isa 59:12</reference>, etc. It is a question, however, whether by זבובי מות, death-bringing, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, poisonous flies (lxx, Targ.,  Luther)<note placement="foot">The Targ. interprets, as the Talm. and Mid. do, deadly flies as a figure of the <hi type="italic">prava concupiscentia</hi>. Similarly Wangemann: a mind buried in the world.</note> or dead flies (Symm., Syr., Jerome) is meant. We decide in favour of the former; for (1) זבובי מות for זבוּבים מתים (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.4">Ecc 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Isa 37:36</reference>), “death-flies” for “dead flies,” would be an affected poetic expression without analogy; while, on the contrary, “death-flies” for “deadly flies” is a genit. connection, such as מות כּלי instruments of death, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, deadly instruments and the like; Böttcher understands dung-flies; but the expression can scarcely extend to the designation of flies which are found on dead bodies. Meanwhile, it is very possible that by the expression זב ם, such flies are thought of as carry death from dead bodies to those that are living; the Assyr. syllabare show how closely the Semites distinguished manifold kinds of זבובים (Assyr. zumbi = zubbi). (2) In favour of “dead flies,” it has been remarked that that influence on the contents of a pot of ointment is effected not merely by poison-flies, but, generally, by flies that have fallen into it. <div eID="gen12365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12366" type="x-p"/> But since the oil mixed with perfumes may also be of the kind which, instead of being changed by a dead body, much rather embalms it; so it does not surprise us that the exciter of fermentation is thus drastically described by μυῖαι θανατοῦσαι (lxx); it happens, besides, also on this account, because “a little folly” corresponds as a contrasted figure to the little destructive carcase, - wisdom בע תּח (“giveth life,” <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.2">Ecc 7:2</reference>), a little folly is thus like little deadly flies. The sequence of ideas יב יבּ (maketh the ointment stink) is natural. The corrupting body communicates its foul savour to the ointment, makes it boil up, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, puts it into a state of fermentation, in consequence of which it foams and raises up small blisters, אבעבועות (Rashi). To the asyndeton יב יבּ, there corresponds, in 1 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, the asyndeton מח מ כּ; the Targ., Syr., and Jerome,<note placement="foot">The lxx entirely remodels <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.10.1">Ecc 10:1</reference></hi>: τίμιον κ.τ.λ (“a little wisdom is more honour than the great glory of folly”), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, יקר מעט חכמה סכלות רב (כבוד in the sense of “great multitude”). Van der Palm (1784) regards this as the original form of the text.</note> who translate by “and,” are therefore not witnesses for the phrase וּמך, but the Venet. (καὶ τῆς δόχης) had this certainly before it; it is, in relation to the other, inferior in point of evidence.<note placement="foot">מכּבוד; thus in the Biblia rabb. 1525, 1615, Genoa 1618, Plantin 1582, Jablonski 1699, and also v. d. Hooght and Norzi. In the Ven. 1515, 1521, 1615, וּמכּבוד is found with the copulat. <hi type="italic">vav</hi>, a form which is adopted by Michaelis. Thus also the Concord. cites, and thus, originally, it stood in J., but has been corrected to מכּבוד. F., however, has מכּבוד, with the marginal remark: מכבוד כן קבלתי מני שמשון (Simson ha-Nakdam, to whom the writer of the Frankf. Cod. 1294 here refers for the reading מך, without the copul. <hi type="italic">vav</hi>, is often called by him his voucher). This is also the correct Masoretic reading; for if וּמך were to be read, then the word would be in the catalogue of words of which three begin with their initial letter, and a fourth has introduced a <hi type="italic">vav</hi> before it (Mas. fin. f. 26, Ochla veochla, Nr. 15).</note> <div eID="gen12366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12367" type="x-p"/> In general, it is evident that the point of comparison is the hurtfulness, widely extending itself, of a matter which in appearance is insignificant. Therefore the meaning of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.10.1">Ecc 10:1</reference></hi> cannot be that a little folly is more weighty than wisdom, than honour, viz., in the eyes of the blinded crowd (Zöckl., Dächsel). This limitation the author ought to have expressed, for without it the sentence is an untruth. Jerome, following the Targ. and Midrash, explains: <hi type="italic">Pretiosa est super sapientiam et gloriam stultitia parva</hi>, understanding by wisdom and honour the self-elation therewith connected; besides, this thought, which Luther limits by the introduction of zuweilen [“folly is sometimes better than wisdom, etc.”], is in harmony neither with that which goes before nor with that which follows. <div eID="gen12367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12368" type="x-p"/> Luzz., as already Aben Ezra, Grotius, Geiger, Hengst., and the more recent English expositors, transfer the verbs of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.10.1">Ecc 10:1</reference></hi> zeugmatically to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.10.1">Ecc 10:1</reference></hi>: similiter <hi type="italic">pretiosum nomine sapientiae et gloriae virum foetidum facit stolidtias parva</hi>. But יביע forbids this transference, and, besides, מן יקר, “honoured on account of,” is an improbable expression; also מך יקר presents a tautology, which Luzz. seeks to remove by glossing מך, as the Targ. does, by ונכסים עושר מרוב. Already Rashi has rightly explained by taking יקר (Syr. jaḳîr, Arab. waḳur, waḳûr), in its primary meaning, as synon. of כּבד: more weighty, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, heavier and weighing more than wisdom, than honour, is a little folly; and he reminds us that a single foolish act can at once change into their contrary the wisdom and the honour of a man, destroying both, making it as if they had never been, cf. 1Co 5:6. The sentence is true both in an intellectual and in a moral reference. Wisdom and honour are swept away by a little <hi type="italic">quantum</hi> of folly; it places both in the shade, it outweighs them in the scale; it stamps the man, notwithstanding the wisdom and dignity which otherwise belong to him, as a fool. The expressive רקח שׁמן is purposely used here; the dealer in ointments (<hi type="italic">pigmentarius</hi>) can now do nothing with the corrupted perfume, - thus the wisdom which a man possesses, the honour which he has hitherto enjoyed, avail him no longer; the proportionally small portion of folly which has become an ingredient in his personality gives him the character of a fool, and operates to his dishonour. Knobel construes rightly; but his explanation (also of Heiligst., Elst., Ginsb.): “a little folly frequently shows itself more efficacious and fruitful than the wisdom of an honoured wise man,” helps itself with a “frequently” inserted, and weakens מך to a subordinated idea, and is opposed to the figure, which requires a personality.
entries.af3e0493f72fa02dcb37ff0fb5fc5fa7e8efb8c2: <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.2-Eccl.10.3">Ecc 10:2-3</reference> <div eID="gen12368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12369" type="x-p"/> A double proverb regarding wisdom and folly in their difference: “The heart of a wise man is directed to his right hand, and the heart of the fool to his left. And also on the way where a fool goeth, there his heart faileth him, and he saith to all that he is a fool.” Most interpreters translate: The heart of the wise man is at his right hand, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it is in the right place. But this designation, meant figuratively and yet sounding anatomically, would be in bad taste<note placement="foot">Christ. Fried. Bauer (1732) explains as we do, and remarks, “If we translate: the heart of the wise is at his right hand, but the heart of the fool at his left, it appears as if the heart of the prudent and of the foolish must have a different position in the human body, thus affording to the profane ground for mockery.”</note> in this distinguishing double form (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on the contrary, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.14">Ecc 2:14</reference>). The ל is that of direction;<note placement="foot">Accordingly, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.2">Ecc 10:2</reference> has become a Jewish saying with reference to the study of a book (this thought of as Heb.): The wise always turn over the leaves backwards, repeating that which has been read; the fool forwards, superficially anticipating that which has not yet been read, and scarcely able to wait for the end.</note> and that which is situated to the right of a man is figuratively a designation of the right; and that to the left, a designation of the wrong. The designation proceeds from a different idea from that at <reference osisRef="Deut.5.32">Deu 5:32</reference>, etc.; that which lies to the right, as that lying at a man’s right hand, is that to which his calling and duty point him; השׂ denotes, in the later Hebrew, “to turn oneself to the wrong side.”
entries.5d604a9ef88841001723039a0abad2cfd83f8cce: <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.4">Ecc 10:4</reference> <div eID="gen12370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12371" type="x-p"/> This verse shows what is the wise conduct of a subject, and particularly of a servant, when the anger of the ruler breaks forth: “If the ill-humour of the ruler rise up against thee, do not leave thy post; for patience leaves out great sins.” Luther connects <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.4">Ecc 10:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.3">Ecc 10:3</reference> by “therefore;” for by the potentate he understands such an one as, himself a fool, holds all who contradict him to be fools: then it is best to let his folly rage on. But the מושׁל is a different person from the סכל; and מק אל־תּנּח does not mean, “let not yourself get into a passion,” or, as he more accurately explains in the <hi type="italic">Annotationes</hi>: “remain self-possessed” (similarly Hitzig: lose not thy mental state of composure), but, in conformity with תלך ... אל, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.3">Ecc 8:3</reference>, “forsake not the post (synon. מצּב and מעמד, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.19">Isa 22:19</reference>, cf. 23) which thou hast received.” The person addressed is thus represented not merely as a subject, but officially as a subordinate officer: if the ruler’s displeasure (רוּח, as at Jdg 8:3; <reference osisRef="Prov.29.11">Pro 29:11</reference>) rises up against him (עלה, as elsewhere; cf. אף, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.21">Psa 73:21</reference>; or חמה, <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.20">2Sa 11:20</reference>), he ought not, in the consciousness that he does not merit his displeasure, hastily give up his situation which has been entrusted to him and renounce submission; for patience, gentleness (regarding מרפּא, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.12.18">Pro 12:18</reference>) 'גּד ... 'ין. <div eID="gen12371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12372" type="x-p"/> This concluding clause of the verse is usually translated: “It appeaseth (pacifieth) great sins” (lxx καταπαύσει, Symm. παύσει). The phrase (חמה) אף הניח is not to be compared, for it signifies quieting by an exhausting outbreak; on the contrary, יניח in the passage before us must signify quieting, as the preventing of an outbreak (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.15.1">Pro 15:1</reference>).
